items.title: The order of 15 modulo 36
items.prose: Work in $\mathbb{Z}_{36}$ under addition. The order of $a$ is the least $k \ge 1$ with $ka \equiv 0 \pmod{36}$.
items.question: Two questions on $H = \langle 15 \rangle$.

feedback.correct: $12 \times 15 = 180 = 5 \times 36$, and no smaller multiple of 15 is a multiple of 36.
feedback.generic: Find the least $k$ with $36 \mid 15k$.

byKey.lcm: You gave $\operatorname{lcm}(15, 36) = 180$, the first multiple of 15 that is $\equiv 0$. The order counts the copies: $180 = 12 \times 15$.

parts.question: How many cosets $a + H$ does $H = \langle 15 \rangle$ have in $\mathbb{Z}_{36}$?

feedback.generic: The cosets split $\mathbb{Z}_{36}$ into pieces of size $|H|$.

byKey.order: You gave $|H| = 12$, the size of each coset. The number of cosets is $\tfrac{36}{12}$.

explain.text: $36 \mid 15k$ means $12 \mid 5k$, so $12 \mid k$, since $\gcd(5, 12) = 1$. So $H = \langle 15 \rangle$ has 12 elements, the multiples of 3. Its cosets $H$, $1 + H$ and $2 + H$ split the 36 residues into 3 pieces of 12.

items.title: A permutation from its bottom row
items.prose: A permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1, \dots, 6\}$ has bottom row $3, 5, 1, 2, 6, 4$. So $\sigma(1) = 3$, $\sigma(2) = 5$, and so on.
items.question: What is the order of $\sigma$?

feedback.generic: Follow 1 until it returns, then start again at the first point not yet used.

byKey.product: You multiplied the cycle lengths, $2 \times 4 = 8$. The order is their lcm, 4.
byKey.sum: You added the cycle lengths. That counts the points moved, not the order.

explain.text: Following each point gives $\sigma = (1\,3)(2\,5\,6\,4)$. Disjoint cycles commute, so $\sigma^k = e$ exactly when both lengths divide $k$. The least such $k$ is $\operatorname{lcm}(2, 4) = 4$.

items.title: Zero divisors modulo 14
items.prose: A zero divisor is an $a \ne 0$ with $ab = 0$ for some $b \ne 0$. Work in the ring $\mathbb{Z}_{14}$.
items.question: How many zero divisors does $\mathbb{Z}_{14}$ have?

feedback.correct: They are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 7: the non-zero $a$ with $\gcd(a, 14) > 1$.
feedback.generic: Test $\gcd(a, 14)$ for each non-zero $a$.

byKey.evens: You counted the 6 even residues only. $7 \times 2 = 14 \equiv 0$, so 7 is one too.
byKey.zero: You counted 0 as well, giving 8. A zero divisor must be non-zero.

explain.text: If $d = \gcd(a, 14) > 1$, then $a \cdot \tfrac{14}{d} \equiv 0$ with $\tfrac{14}{d} \ne 0$. If $\gcd(a, 14) = 1$, then $a$ is a unit, and a unit is never a zero divisor. So the 13 non-zero residues split into 6 units and 7 zero divisors.

items.title: A distance with a jump
items.prose: On $\mathbb{R}$ put $d(x, x) = 0$, and $d(x, y) = |x - y| + 1$ when $x \ne y$.
items.question: Is $d$ a metric?

options.text: Yes: all three axioms hold, the triangle inequality included.
No: the triangle inequality fails, since two hops add 1 twice.
options.why: You counted the extra 1 as a cost to the left side. Two hops add 2 on the right and only 1 on the left.

options.text: No: $d(x, x)$ should be 0, and the $+1$ spoils it.
options.why: You missed the first case. $d(x, x) = 0$ by definition, and the $+1$ applies only to distinct points.

options.text: No: a metric needs $d(x, y) \to 0$ as $y \to x$.
options.why: You added a rule that is not an axiom. The discrete metric also jumps, and it is a metric.

feedback.correct: The $+1$ only ever helps the right side of the triangle inequality.
feedback.generic: Check $d(x, x)$, symmetry, then the triangle inequality with $y$ equal to $x$, equal to $z$, or neither.

explain.text: The first case gives $d(x, x) = 0$, and $d$ is symmetric and positive on distinct points. For $x \ne z$, if $y$ equals $x$ or $z$ the triangle inequality is an equality. Otherwise the right side is $|x - y| + |y - z| + 2 \ge |x - z| + 1 = d(x, z)$.

items.title: Pulling back an open interval
items.prose: Let $f(x) = x^2 - 4x = (x - 2)^2 - 4$ on $\mathbb{R}$, and $V = (-3, 5)$, an open set.
items.question: What is $f^{-1}(V)$?

options.why: You solved on one side of 2 only. Each $x$ in $(-1, 1)$ also has $f(x)$ in $(-3, 5)$.
You kept $f(x) < 5$ and dropped $f(x) > -3$. Points near 2 map below $-3$, as $f(2) = -4$.
You kept the ends. $f(-1) = f(5) = 5$ and $f(1) = f(3) = -3$ are not in the open set $V$.

feedback.correct: $-3 < (x - 2)^2 - 4 < 5$ means $1 < |x - 2| < 3$: two open intervals.
feedback.generic: Solve $1 < (x - 2)^2 < 9$ for $x$, on both sides of 2.

explain.text: $f(x) \in (-3, 5)$ exactly when $1 < (x - 2)^2 < 9$, that is $1 < |x - 2| < 3$. That is $(-1, 1) \cup (3, 5)$, a union of open intervals. An open preimage of an open set is what continuity by open sets predicts.

items.title: A topology on four points
items.prose: Take $X = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$. A topology on $X$ holds $\varnothing$ and $X$, and is closed under unions and finite intersections.
items.question: Which family is a topology on $X$?

options.why: You checked intersections only. $\{1\} \cup \{2\} = \{1, 2\}$ is missing.
You checked unions only. $\{1, 2\} \cap \{2, 3\} = \{2\}$ is missing.
You checked unions and intersections but not the whole space. $X$ itself must be open.

feedback.correct: It holds $\varnothing$ and $X$, and every union and intersection of two members is a member.
feedback.generic: For each family, test every pair: its union and its intersection.

explain.text: In the first family, unions and intersections of pairs stay inside it. The others miss $\{1, 2\}$, $\{2\}$ or $X$. On a finite set pairs are enough, since longer unions and intersections build up from pairs.

items.title: An inverse modulo 60
items.prose: $\gcd(17, 60) = 1$, so 17 is a unit modulo 60. Euclid's algorithm gives $60 = 3 \times 17 + 9$, $17 = 1 \times 9 + 8$ and $9 = 1 \times 8 + 1$.
items.question: What is $17^{-1} \bmod 60$, as a residue from 0 to 59?

feedback.generic: Run the steps backwards to write $1 = 60u + 17v$.

byKey.sign: You dropped the sign of $-7$. From $1 = 2 \times 60 - 7 \times 17$, the inverse is $-7 \equiv 53$.
byKey.coef: You took the coefficient of 60 in $1 = 2 \times 60 - 7 \times 17$. The inverse is the coefficient of 17.

explain.text: Back-substituting gives $1 = 9 - 8 = 2 \times 9 - 17 = 2 \times 60 - 7 \times 17$. So $-7 \times 17 \equiv 1$, and $-7 \equiv 53 \pmod{60}$. The check $17 \times 53 = 901 = 15 \times 60 + 1$ confirms it.

items.title: Orders modulo 17
items.prose: $\mathbb{Z}_{17}^{\times}$ is the group of the 16 non-zero residues modulo 17 under multiplication. It is cyclic.
items.question: Two questions on orders in $\mathbb{Z}_{17}^{\times}$.

feedback.correct: $2^4 = 16 \equiv -1$, so $2^8 \equiv 1$, and no smaller power is 1.
feedback.generic: List $2, 4, 8, 16, \ldots$ modulo 17 until you reach 1.

byKey.group: You took the order of the group, 16. An element's order only divides it: $2^8 = 256 = 15 \times 17 + 1$.
byKey.minus-one: You stopped at $2^4 = 16$. That is $-1$, not 1, so square it once more.

parts.question: How many elements of $\mathbb{Z}_{17}^{\times}$ generate it?

feedback.correct: A cyclic group of order 16 has Euler's $\varphi(16) = 8$ generators: the $g^k$ with $k$ odd.
feedback.generic: In $\langle g \rangle$ of order 16, $g^k$ generates exactly when $\gcd(k, 16) = 1$.

byKey.all: You counted all 15 elements other than 1. A generator needs order 16, and 2 has order 8.
byKey.primes: You counted the 6 prime residues. Being prime in $\mathbb{Z}$ does not fix the order: 2 has order 8.

explain.text: $2^4 \equiv -1$ gives $\operatorname{ord}(2) = 8$, a divisor of 16. With a generator $g$, $\operatorname{ord}(g^k) = \tfrac{16}{\gcd(k, 16)}$, so $g^k$ generates when $k$ is odd. That gives Euler's $\varphi(16) = 8$ generators, among them 3.

items.title: Even or odd
items.prose: A permutation is even when it is a product of an even number of transpositions. A $k$-cycle is a product of $k - 1$ transpositions.
items.question: Which permutations of $\{1, \dots, 6\}$ are even? Select all that apply.

options.why: You called a 4-cycle even because 4 is even. It is 3 transpositions, so it is odd.
You saw pairs and called it even. It is 3 transpositions, which is odd.
You took a 3-cycle times anything to be even. The 3-cycle is even, but the transposition makes the product odd.

feedback.correct: A $k$-cycle has sign $(-1)^{k-1}$, and signs multiply.
feedback.generic: Count $k - 1$ transpositions for each $k$-cycle, then add.

explain.text: $(1\,2\,3\,4\,5)$ uses 4 transpositions and $(1\,2)(3\,4\,5\,6)$ uses $1 + 3 = 4$, so both are even. $(1\,2\,3\,4)$, $(1\,2)(3\,4)(5\,6)$ and $(1\,4)(2\,5\,3)$ each use 3. An odd count gives an odd permutation.

items.title: A product of two permutations
items.prose: In $S_5$ take $\sigma = (1\,3\,5)(2\,4)$ and $\tau = (1\,5)(2\,3\,4)$. Products read right to left: $\sigma\tau$ means do $\tau$, then $\sigma$.
items.question: Fill in $\sigma\tau(k)$ for each $k$.

feedback.correct: $\sigma\tau = (2\,5\,3)$, with 1 and 4 fixed.
feedback.generic: For each $k$, apply $\tau$ first, then apply $\sigma$ to the result.

byKey.sigma-first-1: You did $\sigma$ first, which gives $\tau\sigma(1) = 4$. Do $\tau$ first: $\tau(1) = 5$, then $\sigma(5) = 1$.
byKey.sigma-first-2: You did $\sigma$ first, which gives $\tau\sigma(2) = 2$. Do $\tau$ first: $\tau(2) = 3$, then $\sigma(3) = 5$.
byKey.sigma-first-3: You did $\sigma$ first, which gives $\tau\sigma(3) = 1$. Do $\tau$ first: $\tau(3) = 4$, then $\sigma(4) = 2$.
byKey.sigma-first-4: You did $\sigma$ first, which gives $\tau\sigma(4) = 3$. Do $\tau$ first: $\tau(4) = 2$, then $\sigma(2) = 4$.
byKey.sigma-first-5: You did $\sigma$ first, which gives $\tau\sigma(5) = 5$. Do $\tau$ first: $\tau(5) = 1$, then $\sigma(1) = 3$.

explain.text: Doing $\tau$ then $\sigma$ sends $1 \to 5 \to 1$, $2 \to 3 \to 5$, $3 \to 4 \to 2$, $4 \to 2 \to 4$ and $5 \to 1 \to 3$. So $\sigma\tau = (2\,5\,3)$, a 3-cycle. Both factors are odd and the product is even, as signs multiply.

items.title: Doubling from 18 to 12
items.prose: Define $\varphi : \mathbb{Z}_{18} \to \mathbb{Z}_{12}$ by $\varphi(x) = 2x \bmod 12$. It is well defined, since $2 \times 18 = 36 \equiv 0 \pmod{12}$, and it is a homomorphism.
items.question: Two questions on its kernel and image.

feedback.correct: $2x \equiv 0 \pmod{12}$ means $6 \mid x$, so $\ker\varphi = \{0, 6, 12\}$.
feedback.generic: Solve $2x \equiv 0 \pmod{12}$ for $x$ from 0 to 17.

byKey.in-target: You solved $2x \equiv 0$ for $x$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$, giving 0 and 6. The kernel lives in $\mathbb{Z}_{18}$: 0, 6 and 12.
byKey.image: You gave 6, the size of the image. The kernel is what maps to 0.

feedback.generic: Use $G/\ker\varphi \cong \operatorname{im}\varphi$ and count.

byKey.target-over: You divided $|\mathbb{Z}_{12}|$ by the kernel's size, giving 4. The theorem divides the domain: $\tfrac{18}{3}$.
byKey.onto: You assumed $\varphi$ is onto. Every value $2x \bmod 12$ is even, so odd residues are missed.

explain.text: $\ker\varphi = \{0, 6, 12\}$, since $2x$ is a multiple of 12 exactly when $6 \mid x$. By the first isomorphism theorem, $|\operatorname{im}\varphi| = \tfrac{18}{3} = 6$. The image is the even residues, $\langle 2 \rangle$ in $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$.

items.title: A normal subgroup of S_4
items.prose: In $S_n$, conjugation keeps cycle type: $\sigma(a\,b\,c\,d)\sigma^{-1} = (\sigma(a)\,\sigma(b)\,\sigma(c)\,\sigma(d))$, and likewise for every cycle.
items.question: Which subgroup of $S_4$ is normal?

options.why: You took a cyclic subgroup of order 4 to be as good as $V$. Conjugating $(1\,2\,3\,4)$ by $(1\,2)$ gives $(2\,1\,3\,4)$, which is not in it.
You conjugated only by elements that fix it. Conjugating by $(2\,3)$ gives $(1\,3)(2\,4)$, outside it.
You treated a subgroup of 3-cycles like the whole of $A_4$. Conjugating by $(3\,4)$ gives $(1\,2\,4)$, outside it.

feedback.correct: $V$ holds every product of two disjoint transpositions, so conjugation maps it to itself.
feedback.generic: Conjugate a non-identity element of each subgroup by a transposition, and see if it stays.

explain.text: Conjugation keeps cycle type, so a normal subgroup of $S_4$ must hold whole cycle types. $V$ holds $e$ and all three products of two disjoint transpositions, so $gVg^{-1} = V$ for every $g$. Each other subgroup holds only part of a cycle type, and one conjugation leaves it.

items.title: A large power modulo 14
items.prose: $\gcd(5, 14) = 1$, and Euler's function gives $\varphi(14) = 6$, the order of $\mathbb{Z}_{14}^{\times}$.
items.question: What is $5^{100} \bmod 14$, as a residue from 0 to 13?

feedback.generic: Reduce the exponent modulo 6, then work out the small power.

byKey.prime: You used $5^{13} \equiv 1$ as if 14 were prime, which gives $5^9 \equiv 13$. Lagrange gives $5^6 \equiv 1$, since $|\mathbb{Z}_{14}^{\times}| = 6$.
byKey.mod-n: You reduced the exponent modulo 14, which gives $5^2 = 25 \equiv 11$. Exponents reduce modulo the group's order, 6.

explain.text: By Lagrange, $g^{|G|} = e$ in the finite group $G = \mathbb{Z}_{14}^{\times}$, so $5^6 \equiv 1$. Then $5^{100} = (5^6)^{16} \cdot 5^4 \equiv 625 = 44 \times 14 + 9 \equiv 9$. That is Euler's theorem for $n = 14$.

items.title: A remainder over Z_7
items.prose: Over the field $\mathbb{Z}_7$, divide $f(x) = x^5 + 3x^2 + 2$ by $x - 4$.
items.question: What is the remainder, as a residue from 0 to 6?

feedback.correct: By the remainder theorem it is $f(4) = 4^5 + 3 \cdot 4^2 + 2 \equiv 2 + 6 + 2 \equiv 3$.
feedback.generic: The remainder on dividing by $x - a$ is $f(a)$.

byKey.minus-four: You evaluated at $-4$, which gives 6. Dividing by $x - 4$ leaves $f(4)$.
byKey.unreduced: You worked in $\mathbb{Z}$ and stopped at 1074. Reduce it modulo 7.

explain.text: Division by $x - 4$ leaves a constant $r$ with $f(x) = q(x)(x - 4) + r$. Putting $x = 4$ gives $r = f(4)$. Modulo 7, $4^2 \equiv 2$ and $4^3 \equiv 1$, so $f(4) \equiv 2 + 6 + 2 \equiv 3$.

items.title: Irreducible over Z_3
items.prose: Work in $\mathbb{Z}_3[x]$. A polynomial of degree 2 or 3 over a field is reducible exactly when it has a root.
items.question: Which are irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}_3$? Select all that apply.

options.why: You tested for roots, which settles degrees 2 and 3 only. This quartic is $(x^2 + 1)(x^2 + x + 2)$.
You missed the root 2: $8 + 2 + 2 = 12 \equiv 0$. So $x - 2$ is a factor.

feedback.correct: $x^2 + x + 2$ and $x^3 + 2x^2 + 1$ have no root in $\mathbb{Z}_3$, and the root test decides degrees 2 and 3.
feedback.generic: Evaluate each at 0, 1 and 2, and watch the degree.

explain.text: At 0, 1 and 2, $x^2 + x + 2$ takes 2, 1, 2 and $x^3 + 2x^2 + 1$ takes 1, 1, 2: no roots. $x^3 + x + 2$ vanishes at 2. $x^4 + x^3 + x + 2$ has no root, yet it is $(x^2 + 1)(x^2 + x + 2)$: above degree 3 roots are not enough.

items.title: The boundary of a half disc
items.prose: In $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $d_2$, let $A = \{(x, y) : x^2 + y^2 < 1,\ y \ge 0\}$. It is the upper half of the open unit disc, with its flat edge kept.
items.question: What is $\partial A$?

options.text: The arc $x^2 + y^2 = 1,\ y \ge 0$, together with the segment $[-1, 1] \times \{0\}$

options.why: You left out the flat edge because it lies in $A$. Boundary points may lie in the set: every ball round $(0, 0)$ meets $y < 0$.

options.text: The arc $x^2 + y^2 = 1,\ y > 0$, together with the segment $(-1, 1) \times \{0\}$
options.why: You dropped the corners $(\pm 1, 0)$. They lie in $\overline{A}$ but not in $A^\circ$, so they are boundary points.
That is $A^\circ$, the interior. The boundary is $\overline{A} \setminus A^\circ$.

feedback.correct: $\overline{A}$ is the closed half disc and $A^\circ$ is the open half with $y > 0$. Their difference is the arc and the closed diameter.
feedback.generic: Find $\overline{A}$ and $A^\circ$, then take $\partial A = \overline{A} \setminus A^\circ$.

explain.text: Every ball round a point with $y = 0$ meets $y < 0$, so no such point is interior. The closure adds the arc $x^2 + y^2 = 1$, $y \ge 0$. So $\partial A$ is that arc together with the segment from $(-1, 0)$ to $(1, 0)$.

items.title: Two distances between functions
items.prose: On the continuous functions on $[0, 1]$, take $d_\infty(f, g) = \max_x |f(x) - g(x)|$ and $d_1(f, g) = \int_0^1 |f(x) - g(x)|\,dx$. Let $f(x) = x$ and $g(x) = x^3$.
items.question: Two questions on the distance from $f$ to $g$.

parts.question: What is $d_\infty(f, g)$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $x - x^3$ peaks where $1 - 3x^2 = 0$, at $x = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, with value $\tfrac{2}{3\sqrt3} = 0.3849$.
feedback.generic: Maximise $h(x) = x - x^3$ on $[0, 1]$.

byKey.ends: You compared at the ends, where $f$ and $g$ agree and the gap is 0. The gap peaks inside, at $x = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$.
byKey.midpoint: You took the gap at $x = \tfrac12$, which is 0.375. The maximum is where $1 - 3x^2 = 0$.

parts.question: What is $d_1(f, g)$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Here $x - x^3 \ge 0$, so integrate it directly.

byKey.square: You integrated the squared gap, which gives $\tfrac{8}{105} = 0.0762$. $d_1$ integrates $|f - g|$ itself.

explain.text: $h(x) = x - x^3$ is non-negative on $[0, 1]$, with $h'(x) = 1 - 3x^2$. Its peak is $h(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}) = \tfrac{2}{3\sqrt3} = 0.3849$, and its integral is $\tfrac12 - \tfrac14 = 0.25$. On an interval of length 1, $d_1 \le d_\infty$ always, and here $0.25 \le 0.3849$.

items.title: Same space or not
items.prose: Each set is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}$. A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection with a continuous inverse, and it keeps connectedness and compactness.
items.question: Which pairs are homeomorphic? Select all that apply.

options.why: You matched two unbounded sets. Removing 0 leaves $[0, \infty)$ connected, but removing any point splits $\mathbb{R}$.
You matched intervals of the same length. $[0, 1]$ is compact and $[0, 1)$ is not.
You matched two open sets. A homeomorphism would carry the connected $(0, 1)$ onto a disconnected set.

feedback.correct: $x \mapsto \tfrac{x}{1 - x}$ and $x \mapsto 3 + 4x$ are continuous bijections with continuous inverses.
feedback.generic: Look for an invariant that differs: compactness, connectedness, or what is left after removing a point.

explain.text: $x \mapsto \tfrac{x}{1 - x}$ maps $(0, 1)$ onto $(0, \infty)$ with inverse $y \mapsto \tfrac{y}{1 + y}$, and $x \mapsto 3 + 4x$ maps it onto $(3, 7)$. $[0, 1]$ is compact and $[0, 1)$ is not, and $(0, 1) \cup (2, 3)$ is disconnected. Removing 0 leaves $[0, \infty)$ connected, but removing any point splits $\mathbb{R}$.

items.title: Connected subsets of the line
items.prose: Each set is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}$. A subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is connected exactly when it is an interval.
items.question: Which sets are connected? Select all that apply.

options.why: You saw no gaps between rationals. $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ is missing, and it splits the set into two open pieces.
You read one inequality as one interval. The set is $(-\infty, -2) \cup (2, \infty)$, two pieces.
You thought one point cannot split a set. $\{2\}$ is open in the subspace, and so is $[0, 1]$.

feedback.correct: $(-1, 0] \cup (0, 3) = (-1, 3)$, and a continuous image of the connected $[0, 5]$ is connected.
feedback.generic: Ask whether each set is an interval: does it hold every point between two of its points?

explain.text: $(-1, 0] \cup (0, 3)$ is the interval $(-1, 3)$, and $f([0, 5])$ is connected because $[0, 5]$ is. The rationals miss $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$, and $\{x : x^2 > 4\}$ misses $[-2, 2]$. In $[0, 1] \cup \{2\}$ the point 2 is open on its own, which gives a separation.

items.title: Compact subsets of the plane
items.prose: Each set is a subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $d_2$. By Heine-Borel in $\mathbb{R}^n$, a subset is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded.
items.question: Which sets are compact? Select all that apply.

options.text: The unit circle $\{(x, y) : x^2 + y^2 = 1\}$

options.why: You saw a bounded set and stopped. It is not closed: $(\tfrac1n, \tfrac1n)$ tends to $(0, 0)$, outside it.
You saw a closed set and stopped. It is unbounded, and the balls $B(0, n)$ cover it with no finite subcover.
You saw a bounded set of isolated points. Its limit $(0, 0)$ is missing, so it is not closed.

feedback.correct: The circle and the graph are closed and bounded. The graph is also the image of $[0, 2\pi]$ under a continuous map.
feedback.generic: Check each set for closed, then for bounded.

explain.text: The circle is closed and bounded, and the graph is the image of the compact $[0, 2\pi]$ under $t \mapsto (t, \sin t)$. The open square and the points $(\tfrac1n, 0)$ each miss a limit point. The line is closed but unbounded.

items.title: Complete under a log distance
items.prose: On $X = (0, \infty)$ put $d(x, y) = |\ln x - \ln y|$. It is a metric, because $\ln$ is one-to-one.
items.question: Is $(X, d)$ complete?

options.text: Yes: $\ln$ carries $(X, d)$ onto $\mathbb{R}$ with $|u - v|$, keeping distances, and $\mathbb{R}$ is complete.
No: $x_n = \tfrac1n$ is Cauchy, and its limit 0 is not in $X$.
options.why: You measured with $|x - y|$. Here $d(\tfrac1n, \tfrac1m) = |\ln m - \ln n|$, which does not shrink.
You judged by the usual metric. Completeness depends on the metric, and this one stretches gaps near 0.
You linked completeness with boundedness. $\mathbb{R}$ is unbounded and complete.

feedback.correct: A $d$-Cauchy $(x_n)$ makes $(\ln x_n)$ Cauchy in $\mathbb{R}$, with a limit $L$. Then $x_n \to e^L$, a point of $X$.
feedback.generic: Map each point by $\ln$ and see what $d$ becomes.

explain.text: $d(x, y) = |\ln x - \ln y|$ makes $\ln$ a distance-keeping bijection from $X$ onto $\mathbb{R}$. A $d$-Cauchy sequence has $\ln x_n \to L$, so $d(x_n, e^L) \to 0$, and $e^L > 0$ lies in $X$. The sequence $\tfrac1n$ is not even Cauchy here.

items.title: Which rings are fields
items.prose: A field is a commutative ring with $1 \ne 0$ in which every non-zero element has an inverse.
items.question: Which are fields? Select all that apply.

options.why: You took an odd number for a prime. $87 = 3 \times 29$, so 3 is a zero divisor.
You checked the ring axioms only. 2 has no inverse in $\mathbb{Z}$.
You saw that invertible matrices have inverses. The ring is not commutative, and $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ has no inverse.

feedback.correct: 103 is prime, and $(a + b\sqrt3)^{-1} = \tfrac{a - b\sqrt3}{a^2 - 3b^2}$ for $(a, b) \ne (0, 0)$.
feedback.generic: For each ring, look for a non-zero element with no inverse, and check commutativity.

explain.text: $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is a field exactly when $n$ is prime, so 103 passes and $87 = 3 \times 29$ fails. In $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt3)$, $a^2 - 3b^2 \ne 0$ unless $a = b = 0$, since $\sqrt3$ is irrational. $\mathbb{Z}$ lacks $\tfrac12$, and the matrices are neither commutative nor free of zero divisors.

items.title: The best book on a risk budget
items.prose: Positions $(x, y)$ in two assets must satisfy the risk budget $x^2 + y^2 = 1$. The expected P&L, in £ thousands, is $f(x, y) = x + 2y$.
items.question: Two questions on the best P&L.

parts.question: Why must $f$ attain a largest value on the budget set?

options.text: The circle is compact and $f$ is continuous, so $f$ of the circle is compact: closed and bounded in $\mathbb{R}$.

options.why: You stopped at bounded. A bounded function need not attain its supremum: $x$ on $(0, 1)$ never reaches 1.

options.text: Every linear function has a maximum.
options.why: You forgot the domain. On all of $\mathbb{R}^2$, $x + 2y$ has no maximum.

options.text: The circle is connected, so $f$ takes every value between its extremes.
options.why: You used connectedness. It gives intermediate values, not a largest one.

feedback.correct: A continuous image of a compact set is compact, and a compact subset of $\mathbb{R}$ holds its supremum.
feedback.generic: Ask which property of the circle survives a continuous map and forces a maximum.

parts.question: What is the largest expected P&L, in £ thousands? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: By Cauchy-Schwarz, $x + 2y \le \sqrt{1^2 + 2^2}\,\sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \sqrt5$, with equality at $(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}, \tfrac{2}{\sqrt5})$.
feedback.generic: Write $(x, y) = (\cos t, \sin t)$ and maximise $\cos t + 2\sin t$.

byKey.corner: You put $x = y = 1$, giving 3, which breaks the budget: $1^2 + 1^2 = 2$.
byKey.one-asset: You put everything in the second asset. Mixing in some of the first does better.

explain.text: The circle is compact and $f$ is continuous, so the maximum exists before we look for it. Cauchy-Schwarz gives $x + 2y \le \sqrt5$, with equality at $(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}, \tfrac{2}{\sqrt5})$. So the best P&L is $\sqrt5 = 2.2361$, about £2,236.

items.title: Subgroups of a cyclic group
items.prose: Let $G = \langle g \rangle$ be cyclic, finite or infinite, and $H$ a subgroup with $H \ne \{e\}$. We prove $H$ is cyclic. Two lines are independent and may come in either order.
items.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: $H$ holds some $g^k$ with $k \ne 0$, and so its inverse $g^{-k}$. So $H$ holds a positive power of $g$.
Let $m$ be the least positive integer with $g^m \in H$.
$H$ is closed under products and inverses, so $\langle g^m \rangle \subseteq H$.
Take $h \in H$ and write $h = g^k$. Divide: $k = qm + r$ with $0 \le r < m$.
Then $g^r = g^k(g^m)^{-q}$ is a product of elements of $H$, so $g^r \in H$.
Since $m$ is least and $0 \le r < m$, $r = 0$. So $h = (g^m)^q$, and $H = \langle g^m \rangle$.
By Lagrange, $|H|$ divides $|G|$, and a group whose order divides a cyclic group's order is cyclic.
lines.why: Lagrange limits sizes, not structure, and $G$ may be infinite. $\{e, (1\,2)(3\,4), (1\,3)(2\,4), (1\,4)(2\,3)\}$ has order 4, as $\mathbb{Z}_4$ does, and is not cyclic.

lines.text: Let $m$ be the least integer with $g^m \in H$.
lines.why: Without the word positive there is no least one: $H$ holds $g^{-m}$, $g^{-2m}$ and so on.

feedback.correct: The least positive power of $g$ in $H$ generates $H$, by the division trick.
feedback.generic: Choose the least positive power of $g$ in $H$, then divide any exponent by it.

explain.text: A non-trivial $H$ holds a least positive power $g^m$, and closure gives $\langle g^m \rangle \subseteq H$. Dividing any exponent $k$ by $m$ leaves $g^r \in H$ with $0 \le r < m$, so $r = 0$. Hence $H = \langle g^m \rangle$, whatever the size of $G$.

items.title: Where two maps agree
items.prose: Let $f, g : X \to Y$ be continuous maps of topological spaces, with $Y$ Hausdorff: distinct points have disjoint open sets round them. We prove $E = \{x : f(x) = g(x)\}$ is closed. Two lines may come in either order.
items.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: We show $X \setminus E$ is open. Take $x$ with $f(x) \ne g(x)$.
Since $Y$ is Hausdorff, pick disjoint open sets $U \ni f(x)$ and $V \ni g(x)$.
$f^{-1}(U)$ is open in $X$, since $f$ is continuous.
$g^{-1}(V)$ is open in $X$, since $g$ is continuous.
So $W = f^{-1}(U) \cap g^{-1}(V)$ is open, as a finite intersection of open sets, and $x \in W$.
For $w \in W$, $f(w) \in U$ and $g(w) \in V$. As $U \cap V = \varnothing$, $f(w) \ne g(w)$.
So $W \subseteq X \setminus E$. Each point of $X \setminus E$ has such a $W$, so $X \setminus E$ is open and $E$ is closed.
$f - g$ is continuous, and $E$ is the preimage of the closed set $\{0\}$.
lines.why: You treated $Y$ as $\mathbb{R}$. A general space has no subtraction; Hausdorff is what separates $f(x)$ from $g(x)$.

lines.text: Pick an open $U$ with $f(x) \in U$ and $g(x) \notin U$. Then $W = f^{-1}(U)$ works.
lines.why: You separated $f(x)$ only. A point $w$ of $f^{-1}(U)$ may still have $g(w) \in U$, so disjoint $U$ and $V$ are needed.

feedback.correct: Disjoint open sets in $Y$ pull back to one open $W$ round $x$, on which $f$ and $g$ differ.
feedback.generic: Show the complement is open: round each $x$ with $f(x) \ne g(x)$, find an open set where they still differ.

explain.text: Hausdorff gives disjoint open $U \ni f(x)$ and $V \ni g(x)$. Continuity makes $W = f^{-1}(U) \cap g^{-1}(V)$ an open set round $x$, and on it $f$ and $g$ land in disjoint sets. So $X \setminus E$ is open; into an indiscrete two-point $Y$ the claim can fail.

items.title: How big can the image be
items.prose: Let $\varphi : G \to H$ be a homomorphism of finite groups with $|G| = 28$ and $|H| = 21$.
items.question: Which values are possible for $|\operatorname{im}\varphi|$, over all such $G$, $H$ and $\varphi$? Select all that apply.

options.why: You checked $3 \mid 21$ only. Since $\operatorname{im}\varphi \cong G/\ker\varphi$, its size divides 28 too.
You checked $4 \mid 28$ only. The image is a subgroup of $H$, so by Lagrange its size divides 21.
You assumed $\varphi$ can be onto. That needs $21 \mid 28$, which fails.

feedback.correct: $|\operatorname{im}\varphi|$ divides both 28 and 21, so it divides 7.
feedback.generic: The image is a subgroup of $H$, and it is a copy of a quotient of $G$.

explain.text: By Lagrange $|\operatorname{im}\varphi|$ divides 21, and by $G/\ker\varphi \cong \operatorname{im}\varphi$ it divides 28. So it divides $\gcd(28, 21) = 7$, which leaves 1 and 7. The trivial map gives 1, and $x \mapsto 3x$ from $\mathbb{Z}_{28}$ to $\mathbb{Z}_{21}$ gives 7.

items.title: Elements of order 3 in S_6
items.prose: An element $\sigma \ne e$ of $S_6$ has order 3 exactly when each of its disjoint cycles has length 1 or 3.
items.question: How many elements of $S_6$ have order 3?

feedback.correct: There are $\binom63 \times 2 = 40$ single 3-cycles and $\tfrac12 \times 20 \times 2 \times 2 = 40$ products of two: 80 in all.
feedback.generic: Count the single 3-cycles, then the products of two disjoint 3-cycles.

byKey.one-cycle: You counted the 40 single 3-cycles only. Products such as $(1\,2\,3)(4\,5\,6)$ also have order 3.
byKey.ordered: You counted the two 3-cycles of a product in order, giving 120. $(1\,2\,3)(4\,5\,6) = (4\,5\,6)(1\,2\,3)$, so halve that part.

explain.text: A 3-cycle picks 3 of the 6 points in $\binom63 = 20$ ways and has 2 cyclic orders, giving 40. Two disjoint 3-cycles split the 6 points into two triples in 10 ways, with 2 orders each, giving 40. So 80 elements have order 3.

items.title: Squares modulo 11
items.prose: $G = \mathbb{Z}_{11}^{\times}$ is cyclic of order 10. Since $G$ is abelian, squaring, $\varphi(x) = x^2$, is a homomorphism $G \to G$.
items.question: Three questions on which elements are squares.

feedback.correct: $x^2 = 1$ means $(x - 1)(x + 1) = 0$, and a field has no zero divisors: $x = 1$ or $x = 10$.
feedback.generic: Solve $x^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{11}$.

byKey.one: You kept only 1. $10^2 = 100 = 9 \times 11 + 1$, so $-1$ is in the kernel too.
byKey.image: You gave 5, the size of the image. The kernel is the solutions of $x^2 = 1$.

parts.question: How many non-zero residues modulo 11 are squares?

feedback.correct: $\operatorname{im}\varphi \cong G/\ker\varphi$ has $\tfrac{10}{2} = 5$ elements: 1, 3, 4, 5 and 9.
feedback.generic: Use the first isomorphism theorem with the kernel you found.

byKey.onto: You assumed squaring is onto, giving 10. Its kernel has 2 elements, so it is two-to-one.
byKey.with-zero: You counted 0 as well, giving 6. Among the non-zero residues there are 5 squares.

parts.question: Now let $\psi(x) = x^5$. Each square $y = x^2$ has $\psi(y) = x^{10} = 1$, and $x^5 = 1$ has at most 5 roots in the field $\mathbb{Z}_{11}$. So the squares are exactly $\ker\psi$. Which of 2 and 3 is a square modulo 11?

options.why: You read $2^5 \equiv 10$ as a pass. Squares give exactly 1, and $10 \equiv -1$.
You assumed every element is a square. Only 5 of the 10 are.
You expected squares to look like squares in $\mathbb{Z}$. But $5^2 = 25 \equiv 3$.

feedback.correct: $3^5 = 243 = 22 \times 11 + 1$, so 3 is a square, and indeed $5^2 \equiv 3$. But $2^5 = 32 \equiv -1$.
feedback.generic: Work out $2^5$ and $3^5$ modulo 11.

explain.text: The kernel of squaring is $\{1, 10\}$, the roots of $x^2 = 1$ in a field. By the first isomorphism theorem the image has $\tfrac{10}{2} = 5$ elements. Those squares are exactly where $x^5 = 1$, so 3 is a square and 2 is not.

items.title: A contraction of the plane
items.prose: On $\mathbb{R}^2$ let $T(x, y) = (\tfrac13 \sin y + 2,\ \tfrac14 \cos x)$. $(\mathbb{R}^2, d_\infty)$ is complete. By the mean value theorem, the first coordinate of $T$ moves by at most $\tfrac13|y - y'|$. The second moves by at most $\tfrac14|x - x'|$.
items.question: Three questions on the contraction mapping theorem for $T$ in $d_\infty$.

parts.question: What constant $q$ do these bounds give, so that $d_\infty(T(p), T(p')) \le q\,d_\infty(p, p')$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Each coordinate gap is at most $\tfrac13 d_\infty(p, p')$, and $d_\infty$ takes the larger gap, so $q = \tfrac13$.
feedback.generic: Bound each coordinate of $T(p) - T(p')$ by a multiple of $d_\infty(p, p')$, then take the larger.

byKey.sum: You added the constants, which gives 0.5833. $d_\infty$ takes the larger coordinate gap, so the constants combine by max.
byKey.product: You multiplied the constants, which gives 0.0833. That is the rate over two steps of one coordinate, not one step of $T$.

parts.question: From $p_0 = (2, 0)$, $p_1 = (2, \tfrac14 \cos 2) = (2, -0.1040)$. What is the smallest $n$ with $\tfrac{q^n}{1 - q}\,d_\infty(p_1, p_0) < 10^{-6}$, the a priori bound?

feedback.generic: Solve $0.1561 \times 3^{-n} < 10^{-6}$ for the least whole $n$.

byKey.floor: You rounded down. At $n = 10$ the bound is $2.6 \times 10^{-6}$, still too big.
byKey.no-factor: You dropped the factor $\tfrac{d_\infty(p_1, p_0)}{1 - q} = 0.1561$, which gives 13. The factor is below 1, so fewer steps are needed.

parts.question: Iterate to the fixed point $p^* = T(p^*)$. What is its first coordinate? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Apply $T$ repeatedly from $p_0$; each step cuts the error by at least a factor of 3.

byKey.one-step: You stopped at $p_1$, whose first coordinate is still 2. The second coordinate is now negative, which pulls the first below 2.

explain.text: Each coordinate of $T(p) - T(p')$ is at most $\tfrac13 d_\infty(p, p')$, so $T$ is a contraction with $q = \tfrac13$ on a complete space. The theorem gives one fixed point, and the a priori bound promises $10^{-6}$ by step 11. The iterates settle at $p^* = (1.9678, -0.0967)$.

items.title: When a power of T contracts
items.prompt:
Let $(X, d)$ be a non-empty complete metric space and $T : X \to X$. Suppose that for some $k \ge 1$ the iterate $T^k = T \circ \cdots \circ T$ is a contraction.

(a) Prove that $T$ has exactly one fixed point. You may quote the contraction mapping theorem.

(b) Let $T(x) = e^{-x}$ on $X = [0, \infty)$. Show that $T$ is not a contraction, but $T^2$ is, with constant $q = \tfrac1e$.

(c) Explain why the iterates $x_{n+1} = e^{-x_n}$ converge to the same point from every $x_0 \ge 0$.

Give a reason for every line.
items.model:
**(a)** $T^k$ is a contraction on a non-empty complete metric space. By the contraction mapping theorem it has exactly one fixed point $x^*$.

*Existence.* $T^k(Tx^*) = T^{k+1}x^* = T(T^kx^*) = Tx^*$, so $Tx^*$ is also a fixed point of $T^k$. By uniqueness, $Tx^* = x^*$.

*Uniqueness.* If $Ty = y$, then applying $T$ again $k - 1$ times gives $T^ky = y$. So $y$ is a fixed point of $T^k$, and $y = x^*$. $\blacksquare$

**(b)** $X = [0, \infty)$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}$, so it is complete, and $T$ maps $X$ into $(0, 1] \subseteq X$.

$T$ is not a contraction. For $h > 0$, $\tfrac{|T(h) - T(0)|}{h} = \tfrac{1 - e^{-h}}{h}$, which tends to 1 as $h \to 0$. So no constant $q < 1$ works near 0.

$T^2(x) = e^{-e^{-x}}$ has $(T^2)'(x) = e^{-e^{-x}}e^{-x}$. Put $u = e^{-x} \in (0, 1]$: the derivative is $ue^{-u}$.

$\tfrac{d}{du}(ue^{-u}) = (1 - u)e^{-u} \ge 0$ on $(0, 1]$, so $ue^{-u} \le e^{-1}$. By the mean value theorem, $|T^2x - T^2y| \le \tfrac1e|x - y|$, with $\tfrac1e = 0.3679 < 1$.

**(c)** By (a), $T$ has exactly one fixed point $x^*$, the root of $x = e^{-x}$, about 0.5671.

The even iterates are $x_{2m} = (T^2)^m x_0$ and the odd ones are $x_{2m+1} = (T^2)^m x_1$. By the theorem for $T^2$, both tend to the fixed point of $T^2$, which is $x^*$.

Both subsequences tend to $x^*$, so the whole sequence does, from every $x_0 \ge 0$.

rubric.text: Applies the contraction mapping theorem to $T^k$, naming completeness and non-emptiness, for a unique fixed point $x^*$
Shows $Tx^*$ is fixed by $T^k$, since $T^k(Tx^*) = T(T^kx^*)$, and concludes $Tx^* = x^*$ by uniqueness
Shows a fixed point of $T$ is fixed by $T^k$, so $T$ has at most one
Shows $T$ is not a contraction, through slopes near 0 that tend to 1
Bounds $|(T^2)'| = ue^{-u} \le \tfrac1e$ and uses the mean value theorem, noting $X$ is complete and $T(X) \subseteq X$
Argues convergence from every $x_0$ through the even and odd iterates

explain.text: A fixed point of $T^k$ is moved by $T$ to another fixed point of $T^k$, so uniqueness pins it. For $e^{-x}$ the slope near 0 is close to 1, but two steps shrink distances by $\tfrac1e$. So the theorem still gives one fixed point, about 0.5671, and convergence from every start.
